description: Write new Go surface as a ladder: read the package, declare the struct, settle its fields, stub the functions, plan the bodies, fill them one at a time, test what the signatures do not promise, then pass the vet gate.
systemPrompt: You are writing Go inside a fixed process. You do not choose the order of work and you do not write files: each step asks one question, and you answer it. Do only what the current step asks, even when you can already see the next step's work. When a step asks why, answer concretely about this code, not in generalities. Every exported identifier carries a godoc comment starting with its name. No package-level mutable state.
orientation: How a walk works. You have exactly one tool, `answer`, for every step of this walk. A step gives you what you need to see, tells you what to decide, names the payload it collects, and lists the options you may choose between. You call `answer` once with the option you chose, why you chose it, and that step's payload. The engine applies the payload to the file and runs the step's checks; you never write the file yourself, and you never need to think about formatting. If a payload is rejected or a check fails you stay in the step and answer again with a correction. Every step also offers `escape`, which ends the walk when no option fits the work the objective actually needs. Prose outside an `answer` call moves nothing.

nodes.prompt:
Objective: {{task}}

Step 1 of the ladder: orient. Below are the package's documentation and its existing sources. Learn what the package already owns and the naming and comment conventions its code follows. Decide nothing else yet.
nodes.why: What does this package already own, and which convention will the new code match?

edges.description: You know the package, its existing types, and its conventions.

nodes.prompt:
Objective: {{task}}

Step 2: declare exactly one struct for the objective, in its own file, with a godoc comment on the type. Name the file and the type only. Fields, methods, and bodies belong to later steps.
nodes.why: Why does this struct need to exist, what does it own that no existing type owns, and why is this the right file for it?

edges.description: The struct type exists with its godoc comment.

nodes.why: Why is each field required, and why is this set complete rather than one field larger or smaller?

edges.description: You want to see the field set rendered and judge it once more.

nodes.prompt:
Objective: {{task}}

Step 4: declare the functions and methods this type needs, each with its godoc comment and its final signature. Include the constructor. The engine writes the bodies as `panic("not implemented")`; you write no logic here.
nodes.why: Why is this the right function set and these the right signatures, and what did you deliberately leave out?

edges.description: Every stub compiles with its godoc comment and final signature.

nodes.prompt:
Objective: {{task}}

Step 5: plan every body. For each function, give the steps its body will take, one entry per step, in order. Design here: this is the last step where changing your mind costs a sentence.
nodes.why: For each body, why does it take these steps in this order, and where can it fail?
Which body did this implement, and where did the implementation depart from its plan?

edges.description: Functions remain unimplemented; take the next one.
Every stub is implemented and the package builds.
A structural signature mistake needs correction before bodies can be filled.
Implementation showed a second type is required.

nodes.prompt:
Objective: {{task}}

Step 7: pin the behaviour down. Write the tests for what you just built, in the test file beside the artifact. Give each test a name starting with `Test`, a comment saying what it establishes, and its body without the `func` line or the closing brace; `t` is the `*testing.T` and the engine adds the `testing` import, so list only the other imports you use.

Test what a reader would doubt, not what a signature already promises: the boundaries, the error paths, and anything concurrent. Your payload replaces the whole test set, so include every test you want, not only the ones you are adding.

The gate runs the tests, so you cannot leave this step until they pass.
nodes.why: What could break in this code that a signature does not already rule out, and which of those does each test pin down?

edges.description: The tests pass and cover what the signatures do not promise.
A test you would defend is failing, so the body it tests is the thing that is wrong.

nodes.why: What is the defect in the body being replaced, which step of the ladder should have caught it, and why does the replacement not have it?

edges.description: The body is corrected; re-run the tests over it.
Another implemented body is also wrong.

nodes.why: What did the gate catch, and which step of the ladder should have caught it instead?

edges.description: The gate passes and the code is finished.
An implemented body is wrong and must be replaced before the walk can finish.
The code is right but something it does is pinned down by no test.
